title: Grade the class, remember the curve
allegory: BatchNorm is like a teacher who curves each exam question against today's class and jots the class average in a notebook, so a student sitting a make-up exam alone can be graded from the notebook instead.

cap.1: Your network aces training and flunks validation on the same kind of data. The weights are fine. One switch was left in the wrong position.
cap.2: Train accuracy 95%, validation near chance. The usual culprit is a BatchNorm layer still in training mode because model.eval() was never called.
cap.3: Classic symptom: a train/val gap on one distribution, with val accuracy sensitive to loader order. BatchNorm in train mode is normalising by per-batch statistics and overwriting its buffers.

cap.1: A teacher curves each exam question against today's class: subtract the class average, divide by the spread. Then she jots the average in a notebook.
cap.2: In training, BatchNorm normalises each channel using this batch's mean and variance, then nudges a running average of each. The notebook is those running statistics.
cap.3: Train mode: per-channel batch statistics over (N, H, W), plus an exponential moving average update of running_mean and running_var. Eval mode reads the averages instead.

cap.1: Subtract today's average, divide by today's spread, and every channel sits on the same scale. Then the network applies its own learned scale and shift.
cap.2: μ and σ² are per channel, pooled over batch, height and width. γ and β are learned, one each per channel: 2·C parameters whatever the image size. ε stops a divide by zero.
cap.3: γ and β let the layer undo the normalisation if that helps. Learned parameters: 2C. Buffers: running_mean, running_var, num_batches_tracked, registered so they sit in state_dict, not parameters().

chapters.name: Down the column
chapters.title: One channel, pooled over the whole batch

cap.1: BatchNorm pools straight down a column: one channel across every image in the batch. All of them share that column's average and spread.
cap.2: Statistics are per channel over N, H and W, so each image's output depends on which other images share its batch. LayerNorm pools along a row instead, inside one example.
cap.3: Per-channel reduction over (N, H, W) couples examples within a batch. LayerNorm reduces over features within an example: no batch dependence, so no train/eval split.

sorted loader: one class per batch

chapters.verdict: model.eval() before validating, model.train() when training resumes.

cap.1: A lone make-up exam should be graded from the notebook. Grade it against whoever happens to be in the room and the marks turn to nonsense.
cap.2: Eval mode uses the stored running stats. Left in train mode on a class-sorted loader, each batch holds one class, so the very differences between classes get normalised away.
cap.3: Train-mode eval uses batch-composition-dependent stats and corrupts the EMA buffers. model.eval() switches module behaviour; t.inference_mode() only switches off autograd. You need both.

cap.1: For years everyone said BatchNorm worked by stopping layer inputs drifting. In 2018 a team put the drift back on purpose, and training still sped up.
cap.2: Ioffe and Szegedy (2015) credited 'internal covariate shift'. Santurkar et al. (NeurIPS 2018) injected shifting noise after BatchNorm and it still beat no normalisation. Their account: a smoother loss landscape.
cap.3: The call: the technique holds, the mechanism is contested. Current best account is landscape smoothing permitting larger stable learning rates. What you need is the train/eval split, not the theory.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Buffers: saved in state_dict, never trained
Transformers use LayerNorm: no batch, no modes

cap.1: Remember the switch, save the notebook with the weights, and you will spot this bug in seconds for the rest of your career.
cap.2: Save with state_dict() so buffers travel with the weights. Transformers swap BatchNorm for LayerNorm, which has no batch dependence and so no modes to forget.
cap.3: Interpretability runs happen in eval mode; knowing which layers change behaviour between modes keeps your activation measurements honest when you set out to understand and steer models.

caption.1: Drag who else is in the room. The pink train-mode line swings about; the teal eval-mode line never moves. Same image, different grades.
caption.2: Train mode normalises by this batch's mean and spread, so one image's output depends on its batchmates. Eval mode uses the stored running stats, here mean 1 and std 1.
caption.3: Train: (x − μ_B)/σ_B. Eval: (x − μ_run)/σ_run. A one-class batch drags μ_B towards that class and subtracts away exactly the signal you wanted to classify on.

where_else: Dropout, the other common layer that behaves differently under model.train() and model.eval()
LayerNorm in every transformer: the same normalise-then-rescale, pooled inside one example
Any buffer: state that must travel with a checkpoint but must never be trained

hamming.what: A layer that normalises each channel using the current batch's statistics during training and remembered running averages at evaluation.
hamming.when: In CNNs such as ResNets, typically between a convolution and its ReLU; transformers use LayerNorm instead.
hamming.why: It keeps activations in a sane range so deep networks train faster and care less about initialisation, but its batch dependence makes the train/eval switch mandatory.

object.title: The curving desk
object.subtitle: Four images by four channels of activation bars, with a notebook switch.

cap.1: Four images, four channels. Raw activations: every channel lives on its own scale, some tall, some tiny.
cap.2: Raw per-channel activations: different means and spreads per column.
cap.3: Unnormalised channels: heterogeneous first and second moments across C.

cap.1: Curve each channel down the batch: every column now has the same average and the same spread.
cap.2: Normalised per channel over the batch: each column has mean 0 and unit spread (drawn around a baseline).
cap.3: Post-normalisation each channel has zero mean, unit variance over the batch, before γ and β.

cap.1: Now a batch where everyone is brighter, say one class. In train mode the bars do not budge: the batch's own average swallows the difference.
cap.2: A shifted, one-class batch in train mode normalises to exactly the same bars. The shared shift is subtracted away.
cap.3: Batch statistics absorb any batch-wide shift: μ_B moves with it, so (x − μ_B)/σ_B is unchanged.

cap.1: Flip to eval mode: curve from the notebook instead, and the batch's brightness shows up. That difference was the signal.
cap.2: Eval mode uses running stats, so the batch-wide shift survives normalisation.
cap.3: With fixed μ_run and σ_run the shift passes through as + room. Train-mode evaluation erases it; hence near-chance scores on class-sorted loaders.

cap.1: Peel back to the raw numbers: the one-class batch really was brighter all along. Train mode hid it.
cap.2: The raw activations did shift. Only the train-mode normalisation made the shift invisible.
cap.3: Raw inputs carry the class-level offset; whether it reaches the next layer depends only on which statistics you normalise by.

predict.q: A batch of only bright images goes through BatchNorm in train mode. What happens to the brightness they share?

options.t: It is normalised away: the batch's own average absorbs it

predict.why: Train mode subtracts this batch's mean, so anything the whole batch shares disappears. Eval mode uses the stored running mean, so it survives.

predict.q: Where do running_mean and running_var live?

options.t: In state_dict as buffers, not in parameters()
In parameters(), updated by the optimiser

predict.why: register_buffer puts them in the checkpoint without letting gradient descent touch them.

predict.q: How many learned parameters does BatchNorm2d have for 64 channels?

options.t: 128: one weight and one bias per channel
It depends on the image size

predict.why: γ and β are per channel, so 2 × channels, whatever the height and width.

object.where: Anywhere statistics are pooled over a group: whatever the whole group shares gets erased.
